description: Team black-vortex from Douala, Cameroon. We’re building Hestia, an AI-powered knowledge dashboard that summarizes, ranks and explains decades of NASA microgravity combustion experiments to inform fire safety on the Moon and Mars. Every answer is grounded in NASA sources with citations. Our skills: full-stack web (Next.js, FastAPI), AI/LLM & RAG, data analysis, data viz and 3D. We speak English & French.
summary: Hestia turns decades of NASA microgravity combustion research into answers that mission designers can use. It is an AI assistant, an experiment explorer and a 3D simulator built only on NASA data. Ask a question about fire in space and Hestia answers from NASA technical reports and Physical Sciences Informatics investigations, citing the exact page of each source. Explore FLEX, BASS, BASS-II and Saffire test runs, compare experiments and rank findings by relevance to the Moon or Mars. Then set fuel, oxygen, pressure and droplet size in the simulator: a model trained on 276 ISS droplet tests predicts the burning rate and the chance the flame goes out, shows the closest real NASA test, and warns when you leave the tested range. It addresses the challenge because fire safety for lunar and Martian habitats depends on lessons NASA already learned, which today are scattered across hundreds of reports and tables.
details:
What it does

  • Ask (RAG assistant). Questions in English or French are answered only from indexed NASA sources: 55 NTRS technical reports, 24 PSI investigations and NASA resource pages. Every claim carries a citation such as [NTRS-20190000000, p.4] that opens the PDF at that page. When the sources do not cover a question, Hestia says so instead of inventing an answer.
  • Explore. Experiment pages for FLEX, BASS, BASS-II, SAME and Saffire with 544 test runs from the PSI experimental tables, curated findings with verified page citations, a side-by-side comparison of experiments, and a Moon / Mars relevance ranking.
  • Simulate. A 3D combustion chamber: a fuel droplet burns and shrinks following the d² law at the burning rate the model predicts, and goes out where FLEX data says it should. Toggle Earth (1 g) and ISS (microgravity) to see the flame stretch or stay spherical. The simulator shows the matching NASA test (for methanol at 12 % O₂ it predicts extinction at 2.52 mm; the real ISS test FLEX-086 went out at 2.56 mm).
  • Search. A Ctrl/⌘ K palette finds experiments, findings, report passages and test runs instantly, even without the AI.

How it works

NASA PDFs and tables are downloaded, cleaned, split into passages and embedded. Retrieval is hybrid: vector search (pgvector) and full-text search are fused, filtered by a calibrated relevance threshold, then a Gemini model writes the answer from numbered passages. The backend rebuilds and checks every citation. The prediction model is a ridge regression for the burning rate K and a logistic regression for extinction, trained only on FLEX data: its K error is 2.3 times smaller than a naive baseline (MAE 0.047 vs 0.107 mm²/s) and its extinction balanced accuracy is 0.78 vs 0.50.

Benefits

Engineers, students and mission planners get trusted, cited answers in seconds instead of days of reading, and can test "what if" atmospheres against real ISS data. Hestia is honest about its limits: out-of-range inputs are flagged as extrapolation.

What we hope to achieve

A living fire-safety knowledge base for Artemis and Mars habitat design, extended next to solid materials (BASS-II, Saffire), partial gravity and smoke detection data.

Tools

Python 3.12, FastAPI, PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector, SQLAlchemy, scikit-learn, pandas, PyMuPDF; Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (React Three Fiber), Recharts; Google Gemini API (embeddings and answers); Docker; GitHub.
